grammar[0].blocks[2].text: In every short past form, *ich* and *er* look the same, with no ending: ich *war*, er *war*; ich *hatte*, sie *hatte*.
grammar[0].fact: Nuremberg’s toy fair, the *Spielwarenmesse*, is the largest of its kind in the world. The toy trade there goes back to the Middle Ages, when the city’s craftsmen were making tin soldiers for half of Europe.

reading.intro: Frau Huber has invited Maya to Nuremberg. She has one wish: the toy museum. In front of every glass case she stops, and Maya hears things she never knew about the woman at the window.
reading.photos[0].caption: Das Spielzeugmuseum: ein altes Haus in der Altstadt.
reading.photos[1].caption: Der erste Schultag, vor über hundert Jahren. Die Schultüte ist fast so groß wie der Junge.
reading.en: Frau Huber: Look, Frau Maya: I had this doll too. She was called Gertrud. · Maya: Was she your favourite doll? · Frau Huber: She was my only doll. We didn’t have much. My father was a baker, we had to get up at five. · Maya: As a child? At five? · Frau Huber: Of course. I had to carry the rolls. I wasn’t allowed to play, I couldn’t swim, I had no bicycle. · Maya: I’m sorry. That must have been hard. · Frau Huber: Hard? It was wonderful! I had a big sister. She was terrible. She always wanted my Gertrud. · Maya: And? Did she get the doll? · Frau Huber: Never. Once she managed to find her. Gertrud was in the flour. After that she was white, but she was mine. · Maya: Frau Huber, look here. In this case: a doll, all white. "Gertrud, around 1950. Gift of Frau E. Huber." · Frau Huber: Yes. She’s safe here. My sister is still alive.
reading.fact: For the first day of school, every German child gets a *Schultüte*: a huge paper cone full of sweets and pencils, nearly as big as the child. Then come the family photos, and in the end it holds more dentist’s appointments than anyone admits.

document.caption: Ein Zeugnis aus dem Jahr 1949
document.intro: A real school report, from 1949, for a girl called Maria in the third class. *Zeugnis* is a report, and the small line in the middle gives the marks: *1 = sehr gut*, and it goes down from there. In Germany, a 1 is what you want.
document.fact: German school marks run from 1, the best, to 6, the worst. So a student who is told *Du hast eine Eins* is delighted, and a *Sechs* is what you hide from your parents. Foreigners who brag about their 5 get long, kind looks.
